Database: Native PostgreSQL verification database only; generated schemas and Redis namespaces cleaned
ChatChecks: V8 settings and account-block tables preserve existing account, channel, follow and notification state; defaults stored for old and new channels
Authenticated owner settings and block CRUD use CSRF, Origin and optional expected-user guards; other owners cannot edit or remove rows
Settings version conflict, exact JSON fields, 100 Unicode words and dedicated 16KB body limit are enforced
Block durations are 600 seconds, 3600 seconds or permanent; self-block, active duplicate, stale version and foreign/missing row handling are verified
Block reason is private; name, handle and reason search and active/expired filtering use real rows
Actual Java WebSockets verify guest read-only mode, server account display name, forged client name/userId rejection and public channel identity fields
One-time ticket replay is rejected; WebSocket product Origin is strict and broadcast path/instance binding is checked
Actual message sends enforce links, NFKC/format-normalized banned words, follow-only and account-shared slow mode across sockets
Blocking immediately prevents sends; unblocking, policy changes and expired rows re-enable actual sends without private reason disclosure
Logout invalidates old socket sends; unit tests also verify replaced principal, absolute expiry, unavailable Redis/policy storage and reused broadcast identity fail closed
A deliberately blocked authentication check does not hold the ChatHub global room lock or stop another client joining
Unblock then settings-change does not resurrect stale block state; old word/link/slow nacks are not re-pushed as current restrictions
Unlinked product-mode broadcasts stay read-only even for authenticated users
Settings and expired block records survive a fresh application instance
V1 through V7 SQL hashes unchanged and checksum mismatch prevents synthetic pending V9 DDL
Notes: Backend HTTP/WebSocket integration uses its isolated application, PostgreSQL verification schema, Redis namespace and MediaMTX API fixture; it does not modify an active OBS broadcast
The previous notification fixture now models distinct OBS broadcasts as old bye, new media snapshot, then new announce; same-ID reconnect and same-source recovery cases remain covered
Account slow-mode timestamps are process memory and reset on API restart; settings and blocks persist in PostgreSQL
Browser/product UI verification and actual main application rollout are reported separately by the root agent
No generic RBAC, message queue, chat message database archive, OS change, Docker execution or production-account operation was added
